title: Data Encoding: Non-Standard Encoding
summary: Non-standard encoding hides command and control (C2) content by changing how bytes are represented before they travel over a protocol such as HTTP or DNS, rather than by encrypting them. The operator and the implant share a private scheme, which may be a lightly modified Base64 alphabet, a custom byte-to-text mapping, or a wrapper that reorders and mixes the payload with plausible-looking fields. Because the scheme departs from the published specification, signature and protocol-parsing tools that expect well-formed Base64 or JSON fail or classify the traffic as ordinary user behaviour. Defenders look for the artefact of a shared convention rather than a shared byte pattern: recurring request sizes, near-constant inter-arrival timing, repeated high-entropy strings in unusual headers, cookie or parameter values that never decode cleanly, and server responses whose length tracks the request body. The reliable discriminator is that legitimate clients emit decodable, spec-compliant encodings, while non-standard encoding produces fields that stay opaque even when the same decoder used by the protocol is applied.

beginner.definition: Non-standard encoding means an attacker changes the way data is written down before sending it, using a private rule instead of a public one. Both sides agree on the rule in advance, so only they can read the message. To everyone else the traffic looks like ordinary web or network requests that simply do not decode correctly.
beginner.whyItMatters: Security tools often spot bad traffic by recognising well-known encoding formats. When attackers use their own private format, those tools can no longer read or match the content. The traffic can still pass through a normal web port, so a firewall sees nothing unusual to block. If you only detect encryption or known formats, you will miss this entirely.
howItWorks: The attacker picks a secret way to turn raw data into ordinary-looking text characters.
The method may be a slightly changed Base64 table, where Base64 means a common way of writing data as text.
The implant in the victim network uses that same rule for every message it sends and receives.
Encoded text is placed inside normal fields, such as a cookie, a header or a form value.
The receiving server decodes the text with the matching rule and replies using it again.
Defenders see requests that do not decode cleanly with the standard tool for that protocol.
beginner.example: Imagine a post office where every parcel must carry a printed label in the official format. Most senders follow it, and staff can read each label at a glance. Two people agree to write their labels in a private shorthand instead, so the words look like nonsense to the clerk. The rule book says nothing about their shorthand, so the parcels pass every check. Only the pair who agreed on the shorthand can read what the labels say.
takeaways: Private encoding hides meaning without encryption, so encrypted-traffic tools may see nothing.
Check whether a value decodes properly with the standard format the protocol expects.
Repeated odd field sizes or timing can reveal a shared secret rule between two systems.

objectives: Describe how non-standard encoding hides command and control content without using encryption.
Explain why it differs from the parent technique Data Encoding and from standard Base64 or hexadecimal schemes.
Identify the network artefacts that suggest a private encoding scheme is in use.
Explain why protocol-aware inspection can fail against deliberately malformed encoding.
Choose log and capture sources that would let you confirm or dismiss this behaviour.
